name: American Gooseberry
summary: Ribes hirtellum is the American gooseberry species, distinct from European R. uva-crispa and from hybrids between them. UMN Extension gives shared currant/gooseberry garden guidance for the Upper Midwest; it does not establish cultivar-specific performance for this species.

identity.short: American species, distinct from European gooseberry
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Ribes hirtellum. UMN Extension identifies American-origin gooseberries as R. hirtellum or hybrids derived from it and distinguishes them from European R. uva-crispa. No cultivar or hybrid is assigned here.

growth.short: Spiny cane shrub bearing individual berries
growth.guidance: The shared UMN gooseberry description says canes commonly have a spine at each leaf node and bear grape-sized berries singly or in small groups. The botanical distinction is American gooseberry; the source does not claim that all R. hirtellum selections share identical fruit traits.

cultivation.short: Cool-climate home-garden guidance; local rules matter
cultivation.guidance: UMN recommends full sun to partial shade, rich well-drained soil and at least three feet between currant or gooseberry plants in its Upper Midwest home-garden guidance. It also advises annual pruning. Ribes planting restrictions for white pine blister rust vary by jurisdiction; check current local rules before sourcing a plant. Spacing is soil-garden guidance, not hydroponic placement.

maintenance.short: Thin old and weak canes before spring growth
maintenance.guidance: UMN advises pruning established gooseberry shrubs annually in late winter or early spring before growth begins. After the first three years, remove the oldest and weak new canes to maintain a productive open shrub; also remove arching tips that could root when they touch the ground. Its mature-shrub cane targets are crop-level guidance, not a species-specific yield guarantee.

harvest.short: Harvest by ripeness cues, not a fixed color
harvest.guidance: UMN says gooseberries are ready when fruit changes color, softens and separates readily; color depends on variety. The page covers gooseberries as a crop group and does not give a species-specific calendar for R. hirtellum.

propagation.short: Seed-starting requirements are not established here
propagation.guidance: The cited home-garden page discusses obtaining bare-root or potted plants and tip layering, but does not supply a seed protocol for R. hirtellum. Garden does not infer seed behavior from related Ribes species.

problems.short: Watch for powdery mildew and check regional rust rules
problems.guidance: UMN notes powdery mildew can appear in some years and locations as a soft powdery layer on leaves; good airflow, open-canopy pruning and removing affected leaves or shoots help limit spread. Some regions also restrict Ribes because of white pine blister rust, so check local rules. These are regional crop-level cautions, not claims that R. hirtellum is resistant or universally restricted.

uses.short: Harvest less-ripe berries for preserves, fully ripe ones for fresh eating
uses.guidance: UMN Extension distinguishes use by maturity: gooseberries picked before full ripeness retain more natural pectin for jam, while ripe berries are sweeter, less tart and suitable for fresh eating. It also documents preserving fruit as juice or preserves and freezing berry clusters for drinks. This is shared crop-level guidance, not a cultivar-specific flavor or yield claim.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The evidence concerns outdoor woody fruit shrubs in soil.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema has no evidence-backed woody-shrub category; shrub and cane form are described in the Plant Profile.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not converted to container or system placement.

light.reason: Outdoor exposure guidance is not converted into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: Black Hawk Black Raspberry
summary: Black Hawk is a University of Minnesota-listed black raspberry cultivar of Rubus occidentalis. UMN describes a vigorous floricane-fruiting type with rich, sweet, firm berries; its home-garden cane management guidance is crop/type-level, not a separate cultivar trial or a guarantee for every planting.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Rubus occidentalis as a species. UMN Extension lists Black Hawk among black raspberry cultivars and describes it as a floricane type; no resistance or performance trait beyond the source description is added.

growth.guidance: UMN describes raspberry roots and crowns as perennial while canes live for two summers. For Black Hawk, the UMN cultivar table identifies floricane fruiting; black raspberry plants form hills rather than the spreading root-sucker rows described for red raspberries.

cultivation.short: Full sun, steady water and cane support
cultivation.guidance: UMN advises full sun for best production and rich, well-drained soil for home raspberries. Its general home-garden guidance recommends about 1–1.5 inches of water weekly from flowering through harvest and support to prevent long canes bending, cracking or spreading; these are crop-level Minnesota recommendations, not cultivar-tested Black Hawk thresholds. Check local climate and cultivar hardiness before planting.

maintenance.guidance: UMN recommends pinching black and purple raspberry cane tips when primocanes reach roughly 24–30 inches, then selecting 4–5 canes per hill and removing fruiting floricanes after harvest. Apply the type-level instructions with local timing; the cultivar source identifies Black Hawk as floricane-fruiting.

harvest.short: Pick fully colored, tender berries that release easily
harvest.guidance: UMN describes ripe raspberries as fully colored, plump and tender, and ready to come off with a gentle pull. The timing depends on local season; no cultivar-specific date is assigned.

propagation.short: Start with verified nursery stock; seed protocol unresolved
propagation.guidance: UMN recommends disease-free raspberry plants from reputable nurseries because viruses can be introduced with infected material. Its home-garden guide does not establish a seed protocol for Black Hawk, so none is inferred.

problems.short: Watch for cane disease and winter injury
problems.guidance: UMN identifies anthracnose as especially severe on black raspberries and recommends open, narrow plantings and removal of infected/fruiting canes as appropriate. The guide's hardiness and pest timing are regional, not universal cultivar resistance claims.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The cited cultivation guidance concerns outdoor fruiting brambles, not hydroponic systems.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema does not represent cane-hill architecture; it is described in the Plant Profile.

spacing.reason: Field spacing is not converted to container or system placement.

light.reason: Outdoor full-sun guidance is not converted into an indoor grow-light tier.

name: American Elderberry
summary: Kew accepts Sambucus canadensis. Extension literature also uses S. nigra subsp. canadensis for American elderberry and notes regional naming/history differences. This species-level profile avoids selecting a cultivar and scopes Florida production guidance to its source region.

identity.short: Accepted species; literature also uses a subspecies name
identity.guidance: Kew accepts Sambucus canadensis. UF/IFAS discusses American Sambucus and notes that the American elderberry has also been referred to as S. nigra subsp. canadensis; its Florida native phenotypes and northern American material are not assumed interchangeable here.

growth.short: Shrub-to-tree form varies across the range
growth.guidance: UF/IFAS describes American elderberry growth form as varying from shrub to tree across North America. No fixed mature height or cultivar form is assigned to this species-level record.

cultivation.short: Regional production findings are not universal
cultivation.guidance: UF/IFAS provides Florida cultivation context and says establishment depends on irrigation, weed control and tested selection. It notes limited documentation and meaningful variation among American elderberry material; do not transfer Florida calendar, yield or cultivar claims unchanged to other regions.

maintenance.short: Pruning strategy depends on site and production goal
maintenance.guidance: UF/IFAS describes dormant-season removal of dead, damaged or diseased wood for backyard/small-orchard management and discusses coppicing as a commercial option with variety-dependent results. This profile does not recommend a universal coppicing schedule.

harvest.short: Harvest and prepare elderberries with food-safety care
harvest.guidance: UF/IFAS notes uneven ripening and recommends sorting green/unripe berries and pedicels. UMN warns that raw elderflowers, as well as raw berries and other plant parts, contain compounds that can release cyanide during digestion; dried elderflowers also need heat treatment before consumption. The sources support thoroughly cooking berries and give no flower-preparation method in this profile.

propagation.short: Cuttings are practical; seed is possible but variable
propagation.guidance: UF/IFAS documents hardwood and softwood cuttings, stolons and seed. It says seed-grown populations vary and that cuttings are usually preferred for easier, lower-cost propagation at scale; this does not mean seed propagation is impossible.

problems.short: Identify material and manage food handling carefully
problems.guidance: UF/IFAS warns that Sambucus names and propagated material can be confused across regions and selections. UMN food-safety guidance clarifies that raw elderberries, stems, leaves, seeds and flowers can contain compounds that may release cyanide during digestion; improperly prepared material may cause illness. Thoroughly cook berries and heat-treat dried flowers before use; this genus-level safety warning is not a cultivar claim.

uses.short: Cook elderberries fully; do not eat them raw or improperly prepared
uses.guidance: UMN Extension's genus-level elderberry food-safety guidance says raw or improperly prepared berries and other plant parts may cause illness, and recommends removing stems, leaves and unripe berries and boiling berries for at least 10 minutes. It advises using a research-based recipe for canning and acidifying elderberry products; this is food-safety guidance for elderberries, not a cultivar-specific culinary claim.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The evidence is for outdoor perennial shrubs and regional field production, not hydroponic systems.

growthHabits.reason: The compatibility schema has no shrub/tree category; UF/IFAS documents the variable woody form in the Plant Profile.

height.reason: The selected source describes variable shrub-to-tree form, not a single species-wide dimension.

spacing.reason: Field/orchard layout is not converted to container or system placement.

light.reason: The selected production source does not provide a normalized indoor grow-light requirement.

name: American Cranberry
summary: Vaccinium macrocarpon is the American cranberry, a trailing perennial vine rather than a plant that grows submerged in a bog. UMass Extension cautions that fruit production requires substantial, carefully prepared acidic, well-drained ground and climate management; this is not a casual container-crop promise.

identity.guidance: Kew accepts Vaccinium macrocarpon as the American cranberry species. UMass describes it as a low-growing, woody, trailing perennial vine; its commercial flooding/harvest context should not be mistaken for a permanent submerged growth requirement.

growth.short: Trailing vine forms a dense groundcover mat
growth.guidance: UMass says cranberry vines colonize open ground and can form a thick vegetation mat. It describes them as growing out of water on land; growth is not represented as an aquatic plant profile.

cultivation.short: Acid soil, steady moisture and room for runners
cultivation.guidance: UMass recommends soil below pH 5 and good drainage; it also identifies winter chilling and alkaline irrigation water as factors in home production. Penn State Extension's Pennsylvania home-garden guide recommends a sunny site, average moisture and spacing rooted plants 2–3 feet apart because runners spread; its stated soil range is pH 4–5.5. Both sources call for strongly acidic soil, but their numeric ranges differ; test the site and follow locally appropriate guidance rather than treating one threshold as universal. Spacing and moisture details are soil-garden guidance, not container or hydroponic placement rules; cranberry fruiting remains demanding and climate-dependent.

maintenance.short: Protect vines from winter drying and spring frost
maintenance.guidance: UMass discusses winter dehydration injury and spring frost protection. Flooding or mulch may be used for winter protection in its regional guidance; flooding is a management method, not a claim that cranberries should grow permanently underwater.

harvest.short: Hand-pick dark-red berries after vines are established
harvest.guidance: UMass notes that fruiting requires suitable pollinators and established vine cover. Penn State Extension says home growers gently remove berries once they ripen dark red and notes plants usually take about three years to produce in its Pennsylvania context; this is not a cultivar-specific calendar, yield promise or universal timeline.

propagation.short: Seed is possible but not the recommended homeowner route
propagation.guidance: UMass says starting cranberry vines from seed takes extreme patience and is not recommended; its homeowner guidance instead explains rooted and unrooted cuttings. This is a propagation recommendation, not evidence that seed propagation is biologically impossible, and it does not supply a Seed Profile protocol.

problems.short: Climate, pH, drainage and frost can limit success
problems.guidance: UMass identifies insufficient winter chilling, alkaline water, poor drainage, winter dehydration and spring frost as practical constraints. These are site/climate conditions, not disease-resistance claims.

uses.short: Tart berries suit fresh recipes and tested cranberry sauce
uses.guidance: The National Center for Home Food Preservation describes ripe cranberries as firm, glossy and brightly colored; their tart fruit can be used fresh in recipes or cooked preparations. Its tested cranberry-sauce canning recipe includes a boiling-water process table with altitude adjustments. That procedure is linked as a recipe, not generalized into improvised canning advice. Commercial harvest months are not presented as a home-growing calendar.

hydroponicSuitability.reason: The evidence is for terrestrial vine beds and soil preparation, not hydroponic production.

evidence.note: UMass describes a low-growing trailing vine that colonizes open ground.

height.reason: No single mature height selected for this spreading vine.

spread.reason: The vine forms a groundcover mat; a bounded species-wide mature spread is not established.

spacing.reason: Home-groundcover area requirements are not translated into container or system placement.

light.reason: No normalized indoor light requirement is established by the selected source.
